WALTER T. COLLINS
IT
IS PROBABLE that no more
loyal Psi
U ever hved than Walter Collins. With
his passing on
August 9 the Fraternity lost
one of its ardent and staunch supporters,
and his host of friends, both within and
outside the Fraternity, have suffered a
great loss.
Seriously ill for more than two years,
and having undergone several major op
erations, the end came in Nantucket Cot
tage Hospital. He had been spending the
summer at his home in Siasconset where
he had been a summer resident for more
than thirty years.
Walter was born in Peotone, Illinois, on
July 10, 1878, the son of Thomas and
Emma (Folk) Collins. He entered Kenyon
College with the Class of 1902 but with
drew after several years and went to work.
However, after one
year he returned and
became a member of the Class of 1'903. A
classmate recalls that, having let his work
slide during his early college, he did prac
tically three years' work in one
year and
graduated with suflBcient standing to be
elected Phi Beta Kappa.
Throughout his college career he was
a leader in many activities, having been,
among other things, a member of the
Kenyon football team which in those days
played, and sometimes won from, Ohio
State.
From the day he was initiated into the
Iota Chapter of Psi Upsilon he never lost
interest not only in the aflEairs of that
chapter, but the fraternity as a whole. His
devotion was unbounded, as it was also to
Kenyon. Rarely did he miss a Psi U Con
vention, a
Kenyon Homecoming or a Ken
yon Commencement. His greatest delight
and pleasure on all such occasions was to
form a
group for singing which he usually
led with his fine baritone voice.
Walter brought to his civil life the
reflex of his Kenyon popularity and effi
ciency. Following his graduation he en
tered the Louisiana and Texas Lumber
Company in Kennard, Texas, and then
the steel department of the International
Harvester Company in Chicago. He was
office manager of the Boston Woven Hose
and Rubber Company from 1903 to 1908.
In 1909 he joined Lee Higginson and
Company in Chicago and was transferred
to their Detroit office in 1910. From 1913
to 1917 he was with A. B. Leach and
Company in Cincinnati and Cleveland and
was transferred to Chicago in 1919.
His exceptional ability as an administra
tor and organizer were instrumental in giv
ing him a
distinguished record in the First
World War, in which he served in the
U. S. Army, rising to a
Major of Infantry.
'
Following the War he became associ
ated with the investment firm of Hemphill,
Noyes-and Company, first as Western man
ager and then as a
partner. From 1941 to
the time of his death he was associated
with Tobey and Kirk in New York.
Walter was
always a leader, both in his
campus days and in his alumni years. As a
member of Phi Beta Kappa, he long en
couraged undergraduate scholarship by
giving annual prizes. As a member of Psi
Upsilon he was
always in office, always
leading his Chapter's afiFairs. He served
the national organization in many capaci
ties, having been a member of the Execu
tive Council from 1921, and its treasurer
from 1924 through 1932. He was a mem
ber of the Committee publishing the An
nals and a
moving factor in establishing
the Room for Archives at the Psi Upsilon
headquarters in New York. He was a life
member of the Alumni Association of Psi
Upsilon, and a member of its Board of
Governors. At the time of his death he
was also President of the Iota Association
of Psi Upsilon. A trustee of Kenyon from
1940, he represented in experience and
interest the widest scope of Kenyon's stu
dent and alumni activity and life.
He was a charter member of the Sankaty Golf Club, the Sankaty Beach Club
and the Siasconset Casino Association, all
in Siasconset, Nantucket Island. His clubs
also included the Bond Club of New York
and the University Club (New York).
Funeral services were held at the Union ,
Chapel in Siasconset on
Friday afternoon,
August 12, by Dean Arthur Dumper, Ken-

general

member of Owl and Serpent (Senior So

in World War I and was later commis
sioned.
Brother Brown is president of the very
active Psi U Club of Chicago, a
past presi
dent of the Chicago Alumni Club (in the
football team days), arid a
past trustee of
the Omega Chapter.
He is the President of Brown Enter
prises, with offices at No. 1 North LaSalle
Street, Chicago, and of the Brown Milling
Company, and is the owner of 39 patents
Dan Hedges Brown, Omega '16, and son
and patent applications in some 37 coun
tries on flour milling and water
cooling.
Tall, broad and genial. Brother Brown
lives in Evanston. He is a member of the
University Club of Chicago, the Evanston
"Club and the Quadrangle Club. He has
one child, Dan H. Brown, Jr., aged eight,
a
proof, he says, that Psi U has something
even when its members approach the halfcentury mark.
Congratulations
The Editor of The Diamond congratulates the Chapter Associate Editors and, inci
dentally, himself, on the fine performance of the former in this issue. For the first time in
his Editorship, and, he is informed, for many years previous to that period, every Chapter
in our Roll sent in a communication in time to he included in the issue. (See pages 15-28.)
Not only were the communications sent in promptly, hut they proved to he interesting
and well written. The Editor is now
keeping his fingers crossed in the hope that the same
fine performance will he repeated for the next three issues. That would estahlish a record
and, possibly, a habit and tradition that would carry over into succeeding years.

ALBERT C. JACOBS ELECTED CHANCELLOR
ALBERT
C. JACOBS, Provost of Coi lumbia University, internationallyknown educator and world-famed expert
on civil law, has been appointed Chancel
lor of the University of Denver, Robert W.
Selig, president of the Board of Trustees,
announced on
June 18. He will be the 11th
chancellor of the 85-year-old school.
The appointment climaxed several
months of discussion and interviews with
more than 200 candidates by the commit-
�
tee for the selection of a chancellor headed
by alumnus Gerald Peters, and composed
of members of the faculty, administrators,
alumni and trustees.
Professor Jacobs, who has conducted the
vast affairs of Columbia University during
the frequent absences of General Dwight
Eisenhower, will assume his duties as soon
as he completes several important projects,
probably in September.
Until Professor Jacobs arrives in Denver,
Dr. Alfred C. Nelson, Interim Chancellor
since the resignation of Dr. James F. Price
* last October, will continue in that position.
"Dr. Nelson was not a candidate for the
chancellorship at his own request," Selig
said. "His 27 years of devoted service to
the University and his assistance in select
ing a new chancellor are worthy of the
highest commendation."
Acknowledging the appointment, Jacobs
said he has accepted the chancellorship
because of the tremendous challenge the
position offers for the development of
higher education in this great western
area. "I see unlimited opportunities in the
University, the city, the state and the
whole Rocky Mountain area for the educa
tion of our
youth to become more effective
citizens of our
great country," he declared.
Jacobs called for the continued aid of
the community in developing the Univer
sity, saying "our independent, privatelyendowed institutions of higher learning
have played a
magnfficent part in the de
velopment of our country and they are des
tined to play an even more important role."
Announcing the appointment to mem-
� bers of the faculty and staff, Chancellor
Nelson said, "I see in Mr. Jacobs a man
who can
give the type of leadership which
the administration and the faculty feel so
essential to the further development of
the educational goals which the faculty
have set for themselves. He will have the
wholehearted support of everyone on the
University staff."
Mr. Jacobs was born in Birmingham,
Michigan, on
May 21, 1900, the son of
Albert Poole Jacobs, a
distinguished De
troit lawyer, author and Episcopal church
leader. His mother was the daughter of an
Episcopal rector and a descendant of
Jonathan Edwards.
He attended elementary and secondary
schools in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and was
graduated from the University of Michi
gan in 1921 "with highest distinction," de
spite an
interruption for World War I
service as an
Army private.
Following his graduation Jacobs was
selected as a Rhodes Scholar and received
a bachelor of arts in jurisprudence with top
class honors from Oxford University in
1923. A year later he was awarded a bach
elor of civil law degree.
In 1924 he was made a Don at Oxford,
the first American to receive a
lecturing
fellowship at the English school. He was
awarded a master of arts degree in law by
Oxford in 1927, the year he returned to the
United States to marry and begin his ca
reer at Columbia.
Mrs. Jacobs is the daughter of Junius
Emery Beal, regent of the University of
Michigan for 32 years. She too was
gradu
ated from that school "with highest distinc
tion." The couple has three children, Lo
retta, a
junior at the University of Michi
gan, and Sarah and Travis, who are at
tending secondary schools in New York.
At Columbia, Jacobs was a lecturer in
law, assistant professor and associate pro
fessor in rapid succession. He was made a
full professor in 1937. In addition, he has
been a visiting summer school lecturer at
the Universities of Michigan, North Carohna, Kansas and California.
The teaching and writing he had done
on family and domestic relations law stood
Jacobs in good stead when World War II
